blocks.md: Every developer needs three things before writing a single line of code: a place to write it (a code editor), a way to run it (Node.js), and a way to inspect it in the browser (DevTools). This session is pure setup — by the end your machine will be ready and you will have confirmed each tool is working.
By the end of this session you will be able to install and verify VS Code, Node.js (current LTS), and open browser DevTools.
blocks.canDo: install VS Code, Node, and use browser DevTools

blocks.md: **VS Code** is a free code editor made by Microsoft — it highlights syntax, suggests completions, and integrates with Git. **Node.js** lets JavaScript run outside the browser; it also ships **npm** (Node Package Manager), which you will use to install libraries throughout this course. Install the current LTS — after installing, run `node --version` in a terminal and confirm it installed. **Browser DevTools** (open with F12 or right-click → Inspect) has two tabs you will use constantly: **Console** (runs JS, shows errors) and **Elements** (inspect and live-edit the page HTML/CSS). No code to write yet — follow the steps, verify each tool, move on.

### The Odin Project — four pages to complete in order

Do these four Odin pages in order, then stop — the next session covers Git.

1. **[Text Editors](https://www.theodinproject.com/lessons/foundations-text-editors)** — install and configure VS Code
2. **[Command Line Basics](https://www.theodinproject.com/lessons/foundations-command-line-basics)** — learn the terminal commands you'll use every day
3. **[Installing Node.js](https://www.theodinproject.com/lessons/foundations-installing-node-js)** — install Node.js (current LTS) and npm
4. **[JavaScript Developer Tools](https://www.theodinproject.com/lessons/foundations-javascript-developer-tools)** — open and use browser DevTools

Complete every step on each page before moving to the next, then return here for the quiz.
blocks.label: Do these four Odin pages in order, then stop — the next session covers Git.

blocks.md:
**Quick verification checklist** — run these three commands in your terminal after the installs:

```
node --version   # should print the current LTS (run `node --version` to confirm it installed)
npm --version    # should print a version number
code --version   # should print a VS Code version number
```

If `code --version` errors on macOS, open VS Code, press **Cmd+Shift+P**, type `shell command`, and select **Install 'code' command in PATH**.

questions.question: When you install Node.js, what else gets installed automatically that you will use to add libraries to your projects?
questions.explanation: Node.js ships with npm, the package manager you use to install JavaScript libraries and tools.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of browser DevTools (F12)?
options: To write and save HTML files to your hard drive
To inspect, debug, and live-edit a web page's code and console output
To upload files to a web server
questions.explanation: DevTools lets you inspect HTML/CSS in the Elements panel and run or debug JavaScript in the Console panel.

questions.question: Which Node.js release track should you install, and how do you verify it worked?
options: The latest experimental release — it has the newest features
Any version — Node.js versions are all equivalent for beginners
The current LTS (Long-Term Support) release — verify with `node --version` in the terminal
The oldest stable version — it has the fewest bugs
questions.explanation: Always install the current LTS release — it is stable, well-supported, and what most tutorials expect. After installing, run `node --version` in your terminal to confirm it installed correctly.

blocks.md:
Your machine now has VS Code, Node.js (current LTS), and browser DevTools ready to go. That is the full foundation every project in this course will build on.

**Next up:** version control with Git — so you never lose work and can share your code with the world.
